prompt.question: A Customer Support Agent runs an action loop that reads a ticket, queries account tools, and replies. During a billing-system outage it began retrying the same failing balance lookup hundreds of times, never terminating, until it exhausted the rate limit. The architect must add the control that most directly prevents this class of failure while preserving autonomy. Which design BEST addresses the root cause?
answers: Lower the model temperature to zero so the loop behaves deterministically and stops generating varied retry attempts each cycle

Replace the agent with a fixed workflow so the retry behavior is hard-coded and the model can no longer choose to repeat the lookup, because removing runtime autonomy is the only sure way to guarantee a loop can never run away
Add explicit termination conditions plus exponential backoff that classifies the outage as a transient environment error and escalates after bounded retries
Switch the balance lookup to a parallel fan-out of three concurrent calls so a healthy replica answers before the loop repeats
feedbacks: Temperature controls token sampling, not loop termination. A deterministic loop with no stop condition still runs forever; this misdiagnoses a control-flow defect as a sampling problem.
Abandoning agentic architecture to fix a missing termination condition is overcorrection. A workflow could repeat the same bug; the real fix is bounding the loop, not removing autonomy.

Every agentic loop requires explicit termination conditions, the absence of which caused the runaway. Pairing a max-retry bound with exponential backoff (appropriate for transient environment errors) and an escalation trigger after the bound combines the action loop with error propagation and escalation design. This stops the storm while keeping the agent autonomous for normal cases.
Fan-out multiplies load against an already-failing system and still lacks a termination bound. Parallelizing a call that fails because the backend is down accelerates the rate-limit exhaustion.
prompt.explanation:
Domain 1: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration
Subdomain 1A: Agentic Loops and Core API

1A1 stresses that an agentic loop must have explicit termination conditions; a runaway loop is a defect, never a goal. Combining bounded retries, exponential backoff for transient environment errors (D5), and an escalation trigger preserves autonomy while preventing cascading failure. Lowering temperature or removing the agent misdiagnoses a control-flow problem.

Tool use is synchronous; an agentic loop is asynchronous

Tool use is the capability; the agentic loop is the architectural pattern where the model chains tool calls based on observations. A single tool call wired into a workflow is tool use without the loop; an agent chains tools at runtime.
Both tool use and agentic loops use structured tool schemas. Agentic loops are not less structured; they just iterate, which is orthogonal to schema requirements.

Synchrony is an implementation detail unrelated to the distinction. Both tool use and agentic loops can be implemented synchronously or asynchronously; the architectural property is iteration with runtime decisions.

Extended thinking improves multi-step reasoning depth but does not specifically address the lost-in-the-middle effect, which is an attention-weighting phenomenon, not a reasoning depth issue.

Replace the float with a shared enum (low/medium/high) defined in a common schema module, and have every tool import the enum so semantics are unified at the type level

Have the orchestrator post-process tool calls to normalize the threshold before invoking, so a single centralized normalization step rewrites every tool's float into one canonical scale regardless of how each tool author defined it

A shared enum defined once and imported by every tool gives all tools the same meaning of low/medium/high, makes drift impossible at the type layer, and centralizes any future change. This is the production pattern for cross-tool semantic alignment.
Guidelines without enforcement drift over time. Without a shared type, each tool's authors will reinterpret the float as their use case requires.
Orchestrator-side normalization papers over an upstream inconsistency and adds maintenance burden when new tools join. Fixing the parameter's type once at the source is durably cleaner.

Domain 2: Tool Design & MCP Integration
Subdomain 2A: Tool Design Fundamentals

When the same parameter appears in many tools, semantic drift across tool authors is inevitable without a shared type definition. The architectural fix is to define a shared enum or schema fragment once, import it across tools, and make divergence impossible at the type layer. Documentation and post-processing are weaker substitutes that drift over time.

prompt.question: A Multi-Agent Research orchestrator dispatches four sub-queries in parallel. One returns valid results, two return validation errors, and one times out. The orchestrator currently aggregates only the successful one and ignores the rest. Engineers complain about silent quality degradation. What is the BEST architectural fix?
answers: Aggregate ALL outcomes (success, validation errors, timeout) into a single structured response, annotate the partial-failure cases, and have the orchestrator surface both the data and the degradation signal to its caller
Wait for all four branches to fully succeed before returning any results at all, so the orchestrator only ever aggregates a complete, fully-validated set of sub-query outputs

Take the single successful branch and discard the other three branches silently, since the one valid result is enough to proceed and surfacing the failed branches would only clutter the orchestrator's downstream reasoning
Retry the three failed branches repeatedly until they all succeed, then aggregate the now-complete set so the consumer always receives every branch's contribution
feedbacks: Silent quality degradation is a fallback-without-signal antipattern: the system continues producing output but the consumer can't tell it was partial. The fix is propagating the degradation signal alongside the partial data — aggregate every branch's outcome, annotate failures, and surface the structured response to the caller. Then the consumer (agent or user) can decide whether the partial result is acceptable.
All-or-nothing waiting sacrifices the partial successes that arrived correctly and may block indefinitely on transient failures. Aggregate-with-signal is the durable pattern.
This is the current behavior driving the complaint — silent degradation. The fix is making the degradation visible to the consumer.

Retrying timeouts and validation errors blindly can spin indefinitely and doesn't address the design problem that the system silently degrades. The fix is signaling partial outcomes, not hiding them under retries.
prompt.explanation:
Domain 2: Tool Design & MCP Integration
Subdomain 2A: Tool Design Fundamentals

Fan-out aggregation must propagate degradation signals alongside partial results, never silently drop failed branches. Aggregate every branch's outcome with annotation so consumers can see what's partial. All-or-nothing waits, silent drops, and blind retries all violate this principle and produce systems that degrade invisibly.

Express subtasks with explicit dependencies in a DAG; the orchestrator runs independent nodes in parallel and dependent nodes sequentially

Increase the tool's timeout from 30 seconds to 5 minutes to reduce retries, since a longer window lets slow refunds finish before Claude ever concludes the call failed

Make the tool synchronous so Claude waits for the response and cannot retry prematurely, because a blocking call holds the model until the refund definitively succeeds or fails, removing the window in which a duplicate retry could fire
Require an `idempotency_key` parameter on the tool, with the server deduplicating retries by that key
feedbacks: Rate limiting blocks rapid duplicates but does not establish a stable identity for the original request. A retry after the rate-limit window still double-refunds. The right primitive is idempotency.
Increasing timeouts reduces retry frequency but does not make retries safe when they do happen. The goal is making retries non-destructive, which requires idempotency keys.
Synchronous tools still time out at the network layer, and Claude still retries when timeouts occur. Synchrony does not address retry safety; idempotency does.

An idempotency key lets the server recognize a retry as a retry rather than as a fresh request. The server stores the result of the first successful execution against the key and returns the cached result on any subsequent call with the same key. This is the canonical pattern for retry-safe write tools.

Domain 2: Tool Design & MCP Integration
Subdomain 2A: Tool Design Fundamentals

Write tools that can be retried must support idempotency so the same operation cannot execute twice. An idempotency_key parameter — supplied by the caller and deduplicated server-side — is the canonical pattern. Rate limits, synchrony, and longer timeouts treat symptoms but do not make retries safe.

100% completion is signaled by the tool's actual return, not a notification. The notification at 100% is redundant.
Clients have control over what reaches the model. Progress is for host UX by convention, not model context.

Prompt-based guardrails are probabilistic and can fail under adversarial input; the destructive-command block belongs in the MCP tool's deterministic permission layer

Replace the agent with a conversational system

Require compaction for every subagent as a universal context-hygiene rule

Short-lived subagents typically do not benefit from compaction — they finish before compaction would matter. The pattern fits long-running contexts.

Subagents that complete a single task usually do not need compaction — their context is built fresh for the task and discarded after. The right design is to size subagent contexts to fit their task without compaction. Compaction is more relevant for long-running parent agents or sessions that span many tasks.
Requiring compaction in short-lived subagents adds drift risk without benefit. Apply compaction where context pressure exists, not as a universal rule.

prompt.question: A CI/CD Integration team's MCP server has a tool that takes 5-20 seconds to complete. Which implementation pattern is correct?
answers: Move slow tools to a separate dedicated server so the main server stays fast and is never held up waiting on any long-running operation

Make every tool synchronous and run the server single-threaded — concurrency is the client's problem, since the client can simply space out its requests so the slow tool never blocks anything important
Spawn one process per tool call to maximize isolation, so each slow operation runs in its own process and never blocks the others
Implement the tool handler asynchronously so it yields control to the server's event loop while it waits on its slow operation, allowing notifications and other calls to flow concurrently
feedbacks: Splitting servers is one valid pattern but is far heavier than making handlers async, and it does not solve the general problem for any future slow tool. Async handlers are the right primary lever.

Single-threaded blocking handlers cause head-of-line blocking on the protocol connection, freezing notifications and list calls behind any slow tool. The server is responsible for keeping its connection responsive.
Per-call processes are overkill for the concurrency requirement and add significant startup cost. Async handlers achieve concurrency without process overhead.

MCP servers handle multiple concurrent requests over their transport, and tool handlers should be async-aware so they yield while awaiting slow operations. This keeps the protocol connection responsive to notifications, list calls, and other tool invocations while the slow tool runs. Blocking handlers serialize all server activity behind the slowest call.
prompt.explanation:
Domain 2: Tool Design & MCP Integration
Subdomain 2B: MCP Server Configuration

MCP servers should implement tool handlers asynchronously so slow operations yield to the event loop, keeping the protocol connection responsive to other calls. Synchronous blocking handlers serialize all server activity; per-call processes are overkill; per-tool server splits are heavier than necessary. Async handlers are the canonical concurrency primitive.

Lower temperature to fill the missing fields, since a more deterministic setting makes the model populate all eight fields rather than leaving some empty
If the model omits fields, those fields aren't in the required array; review the schema's required list and add the fields that must always be populated

Tool use does not ignore the required array; the model honors it, and with strict mode (strict: true) required-field conformance is guaranteed. The required list is exactly the mechanism for addressing these omissions.

Temperature controls sampling randomness, not schema enforcement; a more deterministic setting does not compel the model to populate fields the schema treats as optional. Field completeness is controlled by the required array.

Tool use respects the required array, so omitted fields are almost certainly missing from it. Structured handoff schemas with required fields, optional fields, and types are machine-enforceable contracts. CCA-F guidance favors this design because it catches inter-agent errors at the boundary. Maximum density, free-form prose, and uniform schemas each fail to provide task-fit enforcement.

prompt.question: A Code Generation team wants their SDK app to fall back to a different model if Claude is unavailable. Which characterization is MOST accurate?
answers: Fallback is the application's job — the SDK targets Claude Code; the application implements model fallback logic around SDK calls
The SDK automatically falls back to other vendors on failure, so the application gets cross-provider resilience for free without writing any fallback logic
The SDK natively supports OpenAI as a fallback target, so the team can configure a secondary provider directly in the SDK and let it switch on failure
Cross-model fallback is not supported in any SDK at all, so if Claude is unavailable the application has no path to continue and must simply fail the request
feedbacks: The SDK is the Claude Code surface; cross-model fallback is application-level logic. The application can call the SDK, catch failure, and fall back to another model or service. The SDK itself does not orchestrate cross-provider fallback.
No cross-vendor auto-fallback. Application must implement.
SDK targets Claude Code; cross-provider fallback is application logic.
Application-implemented fallback is fully supported; the SDK is just one of multiple model surfaces an application can use.
prompt.explanation:
Domain 3: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
Subdomain 3D: Hooks, SDK, and CI/CD

SDK targets Claude Code; cross-provider or cross-model fallback is the application's responsibility. The SDK exposes Claude Code reliably; fallback orchestration sits above it.

prompt.question: A CI/CD team wants a slash command that spawns a subagent to run tests in parallel while the main session continues. What does the command template need to include to enable this?
answers: A Bash command in the template to launch a background process.
The command template should not include Agent tool calls — subagents can only be configured in CLAUDE.md.
Add a `parallel: true` flag to the command's frontmatter so Claude Code automatically forks the session and runs the command body in a background subagent
Instruct Claude to use the Agent tool to spawn a subagent for test execution with the needed context — enabling parallel operation while the main session continues
feedbacks: Launching background processes via Bash does not create a Claude subagent — it runs shell commands in the background without Claude's reasoning capabilities. Spawning a Claude subagent requires the Agent tool call, not a Bash background process.

Subagent delegation via the Agent tool can be initiated from any context where Claude is reasoning — including during execution of a slash command template. CLAUDE.md configures Claude Code's behavior but does not restrict where subagent calls can originate.

Wrong: there is no `parallel: true` frontmatter flag that forks the session. Parallel subagent execution is driven by the prompt — the command body instructs Claude to use the Agent tool to delegate the task — not by a configuration flag.

Slash command templates guide Claude's reasoning and tool use. A template that instructs Claude to 'Use the Agent tool to spawn a subagent with the following task: run the test suite in [directory] and report results' will cause Claude to issue an Agent tool call, creating a parallel subagent for test execution. The main session can continue while the subagent handles testing independently.
prompt.explanation:
Domain 3: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
Subdomain 3C: Commands, Skills, and Subagents

Slash command templates direct Claude's reasoning and tool usage, so parallel delegation is achieved by instructing Claude in the template body to use the Agent tool with the needed task context. That instruction causes Claude to spawn a subagent for test execution while the main session continues. No frontmatter flag or Bash background process creates a Claude subagent; the prompt drives the delegation.

prompt.question: A Multi-Agent Research subagent prompt says 'Fetch the most relevant 5 sources.' Sources sometimes overlap heavily, sometimes diverge wildly. Which change BEST improves source diversity?
answers: Increase the source count to 10 so diversity emerges naturally, since a larger candidate set spans more distinct viewpoints and the broader sweep crowds out the heavy overlap
Require sources to cover distinct viewpoints — name the diversity dimensions (date range, authorship, methodology) and forbid duplicates within each dimension
Raise temperature so the source selection from the candidate pool is more varied
Sort the sources alphabetically and take the first five for reproducibility
feedbacks: More sources without a diversity rule produce more overlap, not better cover. The selection criterion is the lever.

'Most relevant' optimizes for similarity, which naturally produces overlap. Specifying diversity dimensions and forbidding duplicates within each turns the selection criterion from a single-axis ranking into a multi-axis cover, eliminating both the overlap and the wild-divergence failure modes.
Temperature affects token sampling, not source selection from a candidate pool. The variance is in the rule, not the sampling.
Alphabetic order is unrelated to diversity. The same overlap pattern emerges.
prompt.explanation:
Domain 4: Prompt Engineering & Structured Output
Subdomain 4A: Core Prompt Engineering

Single-axis relevance optimizes for similarity. Diversity requires multi-axis criteria — dimensions named, duplicates per dimension forbidden. This applies to source selection, example selection in few-shot prompts, and any cover-the-space task.

prompt.question: A Multi-Agent Research orchestrator stores session state in a single shared database that all subagents read and write. The team observes inconsistencies. Which CCA-F-consistent design MOST directly addresses this?
answers: Have the subagents lock the database during every single write
Concentrate state ownership at the orchestrator — subagents read filtered state and return updates, the orchestrator commits
Accept the inconsistencies as inherent to multi-agent systems, since concurrent subagents writing to shared state will always race and the conflicts cannot be prevented
Replicate the entire database separately for every subagent
feedbacks: Database-level locks across subagents add latency and may produce deadlocks. CCA-F guidance favors structural change — orchestrator-owned commits — over fine-grained locking.

Distributed writes to a single database produce inconsistencies. CCA-F guidance places state ownership at the orchestrator — subagents read filtered state and return updates as part of their handoff response, and the orchestrator commits with concurrency control.
Inconsistencies are a design issue, not inherent. CCA-F guidance favors centralized ownership to prevent them.
Replication produces divergent state across subagents — exactly the opposite of consistency. CCA-F guidance favors single source of truth at the orchestrator.
prompt.explanation:
Domain 1: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration
Subdomain 1C: Multi-Agent Orchestration

State consistency requires concentrated ownership — orchestrator commits, subagents propose. CCA-F guidance favors this pattern over fine-grained locking, accepting inconsistencies, or replication. The orchestrator's single source of truth eliminates the consistency issue at its root.

assessments.question_plain: A Multi-Agent Research orchestrator stores session state in a single shared database that all subagents read and write. The team observes inconsistencies. Which CCA-F-consistent design MOST directly addresses this?

prompt.question: A Customer Support Agent prompt asks Claude to translate to Spanish when the user writes in Spanish. The model sometimes responds in English to Spanish messages with English code-switching. Which change MOST directly enforces language matching?
answers: Add 'always be linguistically appropriate' so the model self-corrects its language
Run a language-detection step in a separate API call first
Lower temperature to 0 so the language choice becomes deterministic, since a stable sampler reliably matches the user's language without code-switching
Rule: detect the dominant language of the user's most recent message and respond entirely in that language unless the user explicitly requests another
feedbacks: Adverb without an actionable rule.
An external detection step adds latency and is not necessary — the model can detect dominant language inline given the explicit rule.
Determinism on an unstated rule still produces unstated rule variance. The fix is the rule.

Code-switching messages confuse simple 'match the user's language' rules. Specifying dominant-language detection plus the entirely-in-that-language constraint with an explicit override mechanism gives the model an unambiguous decision rule for mixed-language inputs.
prompt.explanation:
Domain 4: Prompt Engineering & Structured Output
Subdomain 4A: Core Prompt Engineering

When inputs can ambiguously trigger multiple behaviors (mixed languages, mixed intents, mixed topics), the rule must specify the disambiguation method (dominant language) plus the override mechanism. Vague rules degrade quietly on mixed inputs.

prompt.question: A CI/CD Integration team adds Claude Code to a GitHub Actions workflow to scan diffs for security issues. The job must run unattended, fail the build when high-severity findings exist, emit machine-readable results, and never hang on confirmation prompts. Their first attempt invoked claude-code without the -p flag and the job stalled. The architect must specify the correct invocation and result contract. Which design is MOST correct?
answers: Use -p but always exit zero and post findings as a comment, letting reviewers decide whether to merge
Run claude-code interactively inside the GitHub Actions runner and have a background watcher process detect and answer each confirmation prompt automatically as it appears
Use -p but parse free-form prose output with regular expressions to decide whether to fail the build
Invoke with the -p flag for non-interactive execution, request structured JSON findings, and exit non-zero from the step when high-severity issues are present
feedbacks: Always exiting zero means high-severity findings never fail the build, violating the requirement. Human-gated merge is not the deterministic build failure the team specified.
Interactive mode in CI is exactly what caused the hang; scripting prompt answers is fragile and unsupported. The -p flag is the designed mechanism for non-interactive automation.
Free-form prose is brittle to parse and unreliable for a build-gating decision. Requesting structured JSON output gives a stable contract the downstream step can consume deterministically.

The -p flag runs Claude Code non-interactively so the job never waits on confirmation prompts (D3), the required fix for the stall. Requesting structured JSON gives the downstream step a machine-readable contract (D4 structured output), and exiting the step non-zero on high-severity findings fails the build deterministically. Each requirement maps cleanly to the print-mode automation pattern.
prompt.explanation:
Domain 3: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
Subdomain 3D: Hooks, SDK, and CI/CD

The -p flag is required for non-interactive CI so the job never hangs on prompts (D3). Pairing it with structured JSON output (D4) gives downstream steps a stable contract, and exiting the step non-zero on high-severity findings fails the build deterministically — prose parsing or always exiting zero cannot gate reliably.

The job must run unattended, fail the build when high-severity findings exist, emit machine-readable results, and never hang on confirmation prompts. prompt.question: A code generation agent's prompt caching metrics show 95% cache hit rate but overall API costs are only 15% lower than before caching was enabled. What could explain this gap?
answers: 95% cache hit rate with only 15% cost savings indicates the cached prefix is a small fraction of total input tokens — most input tokens are dynamic and not cached
95% cache hit rate means 5% are cache misses, each incurring overhead roughly 10 times the normal uncached cost — the miss-penalty offsets all per-token savings from successful cache reads
The caching TTL has been set too short — cache entries expire before the second hit, making every request effectively a cache write
Output tokens have increased since caching was enabled — the model generates longer responses when the system prompt is cached
feedbacks: Cost savings from prompt caching = (cached_token_count / total_token_count) × cache_savings_rate. If the cached prefix is 500 tokens but the dynamic user code context is 4,500 tokens per request, only 10% of input tokens benefit from caching. At 90% savings on cached tokens: 10% × 90% = 9% total input cost reduction. If input tokens are 60% of total cost (40% output), overall savings = 9% × 60% = 5.4% — far less than the hit rate suggests. High hit rate on a small prefix produces modest savings.

Cache misses incur a cache write premium (~25% above base price for the cached tokens), not a 10x penalty. At 5% cache misses, the write premium is: 5% × 1.25x × cached_token_cost — a minor overhead, not a cost cancellation. A 95% hit rate with a 25% write premium nets enormous savings; no realistic cache miss penalty could cancel 95% hit savings.

If every request were a cache write (0% hit rate), the metric would show 0% hit rate, not 95%. The 95% hit rate is measured data — the cache is working. The gap between high hit rate and modest savings is a proportion problem (small cacheable prefix vs. large dynamic content), not a TTL problem.

Prompt caching has no effect on output token generation behavior — the model generates responses based on the input content, not based on whether the input was cached or processed fresh. Output token counts are determined by the task and model parameters (max_tokens, stop sequences), not by cache status.
prompt.explanation:
Domain 5: Context Management & Reliability
Subdomain 5D: Human Oversight, Confidence, and Provenance

A cache hit rate measures how often the cached prefix is reused, not how much of each request it covers. When the stable prefix is small relative to the dynamic content appended per request, even a 95% hit rate discounts only a small slice of input tokens, and output tokens are never discounted at all. To widen the savings, move more stable content, such as tool definitions and reference material, into the cached prefix.

assessments.question_plain: A code generation agent's prompt caching metrics show 95% cache hit rate but overall API costs are only 15% lower than before caching was enabled. What could explain this gap?

prompt.question: A Multi-Agent Research team's MCP server is deployed in a Kubernetes cluster behind an Ingress. Engineers find that connections drop after exactly 60 seconds of idle time. Which is the MOST likely cause?
answers: The server's tool execution time happens to be exactly 60 seconds, so the connection drops precisely when each long-running tool call finishes rather than as a result of any idle period on the connection

The MCP protocol itself enforces a strict 60-second connection limit, so any connection is closed automatically once it reaches one minute regardless of what the surrounding infrastructure is configured to do, which is why the drops land on such a precise and consistent boundary every single time the connection sits idle

The Ingress (or upstream load balancer) has an idle-connection timeout that closes connections after 60 seconds of inactivity — configure the timeout to be longer than expected idle periods, or have the client emit keepalive traffic to keep the connection active

The Kubernetes pods backing the server are being restarted every 60 seconds on a fixed schedule, so each connection is severed when the pod it is bound to cycles out and a fresh replacement pod takes over
feedbacks: Tool execution time doesn't cause idle-connection drops. Idle-timeouts are about inactivity, not active call duration.
MCP doesn't enforce a 60-second limit. The cause is infrastructure-layer timeout, not protocol-level.

Kubernetes Ingresses (and load balancers in general) have idle-connection timeouts that close connections after a configurable period of inactivity. For long-lived MCP connections (especially StreamableHTTP with notifications), the Ingress timeout must be configured longer than expected idle gaps, or the client must emit keepalive traffic. This is a common operational issue with hosted MCP deployments.
Pods don't restart on a 60-second schedule by default. The Ingress idle timeout is the standard cause for this symptom.
prompt.explanation:
Domain 2: Tool Design & MCP Integration
Subdomain 2C: Advanced MCP and Built-in Tools

Idle-connection timeouts on Kubernetes Ingresses and load balancers close inactive connections after a configurable period. Fix by extending the timeout or emitting client-side keepalives. Protocol limits, tool execution time, and pod restarts all misdiagnose this common operational issue.

assessments.question_plain: A Multi-Agent Research team's MCP server is deployed in a Kubernetes cluster behind an Ingress. Engineers find that connections drop after exactly 60 seconds of idle time. Which is the MOST likely cause?

prompt.question: A Developer Productivity agent helps a team refactor a large codebase across many sessions. Each new session starts without memory of prior decisions — which modules were already refactored, which patterns were rejected, and which open questions remain. The team wants continuity without re-explaining context every time. What is the recommended approach?
answers: Embed all prior decisions in the system prompt so the model sees them at every session start.
Rely on the model's in-weights training to recall prior session decisions — Claude retains project context between sessions through parametric memory, with no external file
Maintain a NOTES.md or CONTEXT.md scratchpad that is loaded at session start and updated at session end with new decisions and open questions.
Store decisions in CLAUDE.md so Claude automatically inherits them as project rules.
feedbacks: System prompts carry static rules. Evolving state like refactoring decisions and open questions belongs in a mutable scratchpad file, not baked into the prompt, which is harder to update incrementally.
Claude has no persistent memory across sessions from training. Each new session is stateless. External files are required for cross-session knowledge persistence.
The scratchpad pattern solves cross-session statefulness. Loading at start injects prior context; writing at end captures new decisions. The file evolves with the project, not with model weights.

CLAUDE.md is for stable rules and instructions, not evolving state. Mixing frequently updated decisions into CLAUDE.md blurs the distinction between rules and mutable context, making both harder to maintain.
prompt.explanation:
Domain 5: Context Management & Reliability
Subdomain 5C: Context Efficiency for Large Codebases

Domain 5, subdomain 5C1 addresses the cross-session memory problem: Claude Code starts each session with no memory of prior work. The solution is a durable scratchpad file, typically NOTES.md or CONTEXT.md, that captures evolving state: decisions made, patterns rejected, open questions. Load it at session start, update it at session end. This file is distinct from CLAUDE.md, which holds stable project rules rather than mutable session state.

assessments.question_plain: A Developer Productivity agent helps a team refactor a large codebase across many sessions. Each new session starts without memory of prior decisions — which modules were already refactored, which patterns were rejected, and which open questions remain. The team wants continuity without re-explaining context every time. What is the recommended approach?

prompt.question: A Data Extraction prompt instructs Claude to 'extract dates in ISO format.' Some outputs use 2026-06-15, some 2026/06/15, some June 15 2026. Which change BEST stabilizes the format?
answers: Use JSON mode so the date is emitted as a clean string value
Provide three examples of ISO dates and trust the model to generalize, since worked instances implicitly teach the exact pattern for every novel date
Lower temperature so the date-format choice stabilizes across extractions
Specify 'YYYY-MM-DD with hyphens, zero-padded; reject any other format' and provide one canonical example
feedbacks: JSON mode constrains structure, not date format within the string field.
Examples without a stated rule produce pattern-match, not constraint. The model can still pick a variant if a novel date shape arrives.
Format choice is a rule decision, not a sampling decision. Determinism on a vague rule produces deterministic ambiguity.

'ISO format' is ambiguous because ISO 8601 admits several variants. Specifying the exact pattern (YYYY-MM-DD, hyphens, zero-padding) plus a canonical example removes interpretation latitude and gives the model an unambiguous target.
prompt.explanation:
Domain 4: Prompt Engineering & Structured Output
Subdomain 4A: Core Prompt Engineering

Format names like 'ISO date' have multiple valid sub-formats. Explicit criteria must specify the exact pattern, not the name of the standard. This applies equally to date, currency, phone number, and identifier formats.

assessments.question_plain: A Data Extraction prompt instructs Claude to 'extract dates in ISO format.' Some outputs use 2026-06-15, some 2026/06/15, some June 15 2026. Which change BEST stabilizes the format?

prompt.question: A Developer Productivity user asks Claude Code to summarize the test suite without modifying anything. Which tool sequence MOST closely matches the read-only intent?
answers: Run a Bash find command to delete cached test artifacts before summarizing
Edit each file with an empty replacement to confirm presence then summarize
Write a temporary inventory file and read it back to produce the summary
Read each test file individually and then return the summary to the user
feedbacks: Deleting artifacts is destructive and unrelated to the summarization task. The user requested no modifications, so any deletion violates the constraint regardless of test-suite hygiene benefits.
Edit is a mutation tool even with a no-op replacement and triggers write semantics. Misusing Edit to probe files violates the read-only intent and may trip PreToolUse hooks.
Write mutates the working directory by creating a new file. The user explicitly requested no modifications; introducing a scratch file violates that constraint when Read alone is sufficient.
Read is the explicit read-only tool. Using only Read keeps the action observably non-mutating, gives Claude precise content access, and matches the user's stated read-only intent.
prompt.explanation:
Domain 3: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
Subdomain 3A: Claude Code Fundamentals

Claude Code distinguishes read-only tools (Read, WebSearch) from mutating tools (Write, Edit, Bash side effects). When a user states a read-only intent, the correct tool path uses only the non-mutating tools, both to honor intent and to keep the action auditable.

assessments.question_plain: A Developer Productivity user asks Claude Code to summarize the test suite without modifying anything. Which tool sequence MOST closely matches the read-only intent?

prompt.question: A Developer Productivity team wants CLAUDE.md to encourage Claude to ask clarifying questions before destructive operations. Which phrasing is MOST effective?
answers: Aspirational phrasing such as always be cautious with sensitive operations, trusting the model to infer when an operation is risky enough to warrant pausing
Explicit trigger plus action — 'Before deleting files or dropping tables, ask the user to confirm the scope.'
Generic phrasing such as when in doubt, ask the user, leaving it to the model to judge which situations actually warrant a confirmation
Inverted — 'Never ask the user anything during a session.'
feedbacks: 'Cautious' is subjective. Without explicit triggers and actions, the rule fails to shape behavior reliably.
Explicit triggers (deleting files, dropping tables) paired with the desired action (ask for confirmation) give Claude a clear if-then. Vague encouragements like 'be careful' are weaker.
Doubt is subjective. Explicit triggers anchor the rule to observable events.
This is the opposite of the requirement. Explicit if-then phrasing is the right tool.
prompt.explanation:
Domain 3: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
Subdomain 3B: CLAUDE.md Configuration Hierarchy

Effective CLAUDE.md instructions use explicit if-then phrasing: name the observable trigger, then name the required action. Vague appeals like 'be careful' leave the model to judge risk subjectively and underdeliver, while concrete triggers such as deleting files or dropping tables anchor the confirmation behavior reliably.

assessments.question_plain: A Developer Productivity team wants CLAUDE.md to encourage Claude to ask clarifying questions before destructive operations. Which phrasing is MOST effective?

prompt.question: A Data Extraction agent queries a database for records matching a filter. The query succeeds but returns 0 rows. The agent reports 'no records found.' Which is the MOST important reliability check before accepting that conclusion?
answers: Verify the agent had access to the table and the filter executed correctly
Re-run the query at a different time of day
Trust the database driver to report any access issue, since a silent driver implies the table was genuinely empty
Cache the empty result so the next query is faster
feedbacks: An empty result and an access failure can look identical — both produce 'no records.' The reliability discipline is to confirm the query actually ran against the intended scope with permission, distinguishing a true empty result from a permission-denied query that silently returned empty. CCA-F treats this distinction as a primary reliability gate.
Time-of-day variation does not address the empty-vs-access-failure distinction. The agent might run the query 24 hours later with the same access issue and same empty result.

Many access patterns silently return empty rather than erroring — RBAC may scope the visible rows to none, views may filter, or the connection may target a wrong schema. The driver is not always reliable for this distinction.
Caching an empty result that may actually be an access failure compounds the problem — future queries return the wrong empty conclusion from cache.
prompt.explanation:
Domain 5: Context Management & Reliability
Subdomain 5B: Escalation and Error Propagation

Empty results and access failures often appear identical to the agent. The CCA-F D5 reliability discipline is to verify that the query ran against the intended scope with proper access before accepting an empty result. This composes with provenance tracking (5D3) to ensure conclusions are grounded in actually-accessed data.

assessments.question_plain: A Data Extraction agent queries a database for records matching a filter. The query succeeds but returns 0 rows. The agent reports 'no records found.' Which is the MOST important reliability check before accepting that conclusion?

prompt.question: A Code Generation team's system prompt has 8 instructions all phrased imperatively: 'Use type hints. Avoid global state. Test all functions.' New rules are appended at the bottom over time. Which change BEST improves long-term maintainability?
answers: Convert the imperatives to declaratives so the rules read more naturally to editors
Number the rules so each can be referenced by a stable index when editing
Group related rules under XML-tagged sections — <type_safety>, <state_management>, <testing> — and assign each new rule to a section
Lower temperature so the rules are applied more consistently, since a deterministic sampler enforces all eight imperatives uniformly enough to feel maintained
feedbacks: Phrasing change does not address organization. Maintenance pain comes from structure, not voice.
Numbering creates fragile cross-references — adding a rule shifts all subsequent numbers. Tagging by concern is order-independent.

Flat imperative lists scale poorly because related rules drift apart over edit cycles. XML sectioning by concern gives each new rule a natural home, makes related rules discoverable together, and surfaces duplications when they appear. Maintenance becomes proportional to section count, not rule count.
Parameters do not affect prompt organization.
prompt.explanation:
Domain 4: Prompt Engineering & Structured Output
Subdomain 4A: Core Prompt Engineering

System prompts mature like any codebase. Concern-based grouping with XML tags is the canonical organization pattern. This bridges 4A2 (system prompt structure) with 4A3 (XML tags) and serves the team's long-term prompt-as-code workflow.

assessments.question_plain: A Code Generation team's system prompt has 8 instructions all phrased imperatively: 'Use type hints. Avoid global state. Test all functions.' New rules are appended at the bottom over time. Which change BEST improves long-term maintainability?

prompt.question: A Multi-Agent Research team uses Claude's built-in web_search and a custom MCP-exposed academic-database search. Both descriptions are well-written and disambiguating. The team adds prompt-injection-resistant phrasing to the system prompt asking the model to prefer the academic-database for scholarly queries. Why might this still fail to enforce the routing?
answers: System-prompt rules are always ignored by Claude, so encoding the routing preference there can never have any effect on which search tool the model actually selects at decision time

System-prompt routing rules are instructions the model usually follows but can be overridden by adversarial inputs or context drift — for high-impact routing decisions, the tool descriptions themselves are more durable because the comparison happens at every routing decision

System-prompt rules only work for tools and not for distinguishing built-in tools from MCP-exposed ones, because the model routes the two sources through different paths a single instruction cannot span

System-prompt routing rules are forbidden by Anthropic's terms of service when they steer the model away from a built-in tool toward a third-party one, so the rule would have to be removed for compliance anyway, and any preference expressed in the system prompt that demotes a first-party tool in favor of a custom MCP tool is treated as an unsupported configuration
feedbacks: Claude does follow system-prompt rules under normal conditions. The concern is durability under adversarial or drifted contexts, not total ignorance.

System prompts are instructions, not enforcement. They guide the model under normal conditions but can be overridden by prompt injection, context drift, or contradictory user requests. The routing decision happens at description comparison; system-prompt rules are a softer layer above it. Description-level routing is more durable because it lives in the comparison the model actually performs.
System-prompt rules apply uniformly across tool sources. The durability concern is general, not specific to built-in vs. MCP.
No such prohibition exists. The concern is durability and effectiveness, not a TOS violation.
prompt.explanation:
Domain 2: Tool Design & MCP Integration
Subdomain 2C: Advanced MCP and Built-in Tools

System-prompt routing rules are instructions the model usually follows but can drift under adversarial input or context shift. Description-level routing is more durable because the comparison happens at every routing decision. For high-impact routing, encode the rule in the tool descriptions themselves.

assessments.question_plain: A Multi-Agent Research team uses Claude's built-in web_search and a custom MCP-exposed academic-database search. Both descriptions are well-written and disambiguating. The team adds prompt-injection-resistant phrasing to the system prompt asking the model to prefer the academic-database for scholarly queries. Why might this still fail to enforce the routing?

prompt.question: A Customer Support Agent receives a vague request: 'fix my account.' The agent must decide whether to ask clarifying questions or to interpret and proceed. Which factor MOST strongly favors asking?
answers: The agent is configured with a polite persona
The user has simply not gone to the trouble of specifying what exactly the word 'fix' is supposed to mean here
The agent has access to multiple tools
The agent's actions are irreversible or high-impact, making misinterpretation costly
feedbacks: Persona affects tone, not the decision to ask. A polite agent still must judge when clarification is warranted versus interpretation; that judgment is impact-driven.

Vagueness alone is not sufficient — many vague requests have a reasonable default interpretation. The discriminator is whether misinterpretation is costly enough to justify the clarification friction.
Tool count is unrelated to ambiguity handling. Whether to ask depends on impact of misinterpretation, not on toolset breadth.

Irreversibility and high impact tip the balance toward clarification. CCA-F guidance favors asking when misinterpretation is costly; for reversible low-impact actions, interpreting-and-proceeding may be fine. Impact drives the design choice.
prompt.explanation:
Domain 1: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration
Subdomain 1B: Task Decomposition and Planning

When agent actions are irreversible or high-impact, ambiguity should trigger clarification rather than interpretation. CCA-F guidance favors asking when misinterpretation is costly; for low-impact reversible actions, proceeding with a reasonable default may be acceptable. Impact is the design lever.

assessments.question_plain: A Customer Support Agent receives a vague request: 'fix my account.' The agent must decide whether to ask clarifying questions or to interpret and proceed. Which factor MOST strongly favors asking?

prompt.question: A Customer Support Agent uses a workflow that classifies the user's intent, retrieves docs, and generates a reply. The team wants to upgrade to handle multi-turn back-and-forth where Claude can ask clarifying questions and call account tools as needed. Which class change BEST describes the upgrade?
answers: Workflow to agentic, because the new behavior requires runtime decisions about tool calls and clarifications
Workflow to conversational, because the clarifying questions are themselves nothing more than user-turn interactions
Workflow to multi-agent, because clarification is a separate concern from tool use
No change, because the existing workflow can handle the new behavior with more branches
feedbacks: Adding runtime decisions about when to ask clarifying questions and when to call account tools moves the system out of the workflow class. The model now decides the next action at each turn — the defining property of an agentic loop.
Conversational systems do not call account tools or take action — they only respond. Adding tools and runtime decisions takes the system into the agentic class, not back into conversational.
Clarification and tool use can both run in a single agent. Splitting them across agents adds coordination overhead without unlocking new capability — the upgrade is to agentic, not to multi-agent.

Multi-turn back-and-forth with runtime decisions about tool calls cannot be expressed as fixed branches without combinatorial explosion. The new requirements need runtime decision-making, which workflows cannot provide by definition.
prompt.explanation:
Domain 1: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration
Subdomain 1A: Agentic Loops and Core API

Adding runtime decisions about which tools to call and when to ask the user for clarification moves a workflow into the agentic class. The model now drives the next action at each step, which is the defining property of an agent — fixed branches cannot scale to this requirement.

prompt.question: A Data Extraction team uses Claude Code to read large vendor invoices and write normalized records. Sessions degrade after an hour: Claude forgets earlier extraction rules and re-reads processed files. The lead suspects repeated Read results are crowding out the standing rules. Given how the Claude Code execution model accumulates tool output in the session context window, which redesign MOST directly addresses the root cause?
answers: Lower the temperature on the underlying model calls so extraction becomes more deterministic and Claude stops re-reading files, since lower sampling randomness makes the model recall earlier rules more reliably and avoid redundant tool calls as the session grows
Move the extraction rules into the user-level CLAUDE.md so they are reloaded automatically and cannot be forgotten mid-session
Delegate the verbose per-file reading to subagents that return only the extracted fields, keeping bulky Read output out of the parent session context
Increase the size of each Read call so fewer total calls are needed, reducing the number of tool results stored in context
feedbacks: Temperature controls sampling randomness, not context window occupancy. The forgetting is caused by accumulated tool output displacing earlier content, which sampling parameters do not affect.

CLAUDE.md is loaded once at session start and itself counts against the context window. It is not re-injected as the window fills, so it does not prevent rules from being compacted out by tool output.

In Claude Code's execution model, every Read result accumulates in the session context window and can push out standing rules. Subagent delegation isolates verbose discovery (D5) so the parent receives only compact results, preserving the rules and session continuity. This pairs the tool execution model (D3) with context-efficiency design (D5).
Larger reads put MORE bytes of tool output into the context window per call, accelerating the displacement of earlier rules rather than relieving it.

Claude Code accumulates every tool result in the session context window, so verbose Read output can crowd out standing rules and cause re-reading. Temperature, CLAUDE.md reloading, and larger reads do not address context occupancy.

prompt.question: A CI/CD Integration job uses Claude to summarize nightly build logs. The 500MB log is chunked into 250 chunks and processed serially, with each call's output passed forward as context. By chunk 50, summaries become generic. Which factor BEST explains it?
answers: Build logs at chunk 50 contain no useful information
The model's training data does not include build logs, so by chunk 50 it is generating from priors rather than the specific log content in context
Accumulated prior summaries dominate context and dilute the new chunk's signal
JSON mode is rate-limiting the output, so the structured-format overhead throttles each call and the summaries thin out as the throttle tightens
feedbacks: The stem describes a systematic decay pattern starting at chunk 50, not a content gap. Real logs of that size contain useful information throughout.

Training-data coverage does not explain a quality decay that appears specifically after chunk 50. If the model could summarize early chunks well, the architecture, not the training corpus, is the cause of the degradation.

Carrying every prior summary forward grows the running context with each chunk, eventually overwhelming the current chunk's signal. The model attends increasingly to prior summaries rather than the new log content, producing generic, recap-style output rather than fresh, log-specific findings.
JSON mode constrains output shape, not summary specificity. The stem does not mention JSON mode and rate limits would produce errors, not generic content.
prompt.explanation:

Subdomain 5A: Context Preservation

Append-only context accumulation in long pipelines is a classic D5 anti-pattern. The fix is to summarize the running summary periodically (compaction) or to design chunks as context-isolated so the model focuses on each chunk in turn, only synthesizing at the end.

Drop confidence scoring and instead gate auto-merge purely on whether the generated code compiles cleanly
Train the model further on edge cases until its confidence becomes reliable

Calibration against a labeled validation set establishes the mapping (e.g., model-reported 0.9 maps to actual 70% accuracy). Without calibration, the score is a noisy signal; with calibration, it becomes operationally useful.
Trusting uncalibrated confidence is exactly the failure mode the team observed. Trust requires calibration first.
Calibration is the fix; dropping the signal removes a useful routing dimension.
Further training is heavy and does not directly address calibration. A calibration step uses the existing model with a measured mapping.

-p disables CLAUDE.md loading entirely to keep CI runs lean, so non-interactive pipeline runs deliberately start without any project configuration
Each -p invocation is a fresh session — no state from prior -p runs carries over unless reloaded from files

There is no implicit cross-invocation session for -p. Each call is its own context. Working directory affects file resolution, not session continuity.

Claude violated the constraint — any tool call counts as touching files
Read is non-mutating and does not violate the do-not-touch constraint — file content is unchanged
Read mutates the file's access time metadata so it counts as a modification
feedbacks: Read is not forbidden by a do-not-touch constraint focused on mutation. Forbidding all tools is a different, stricter request the user did not make.
Read is read-only by definition. Treating any tool call as a violation conflates 'tool use' with 'mutation' and misrepresents Claude Code's tool model.

Read does not modify files; it loads content into context. 'Don't touch any files' typically refers to mutation, which Read does not cause. The constraint is upheld even when Claude grounds the answer by reading.
atime updates are filesystem metadata that users almost never mean when they say 'touch any files.' Treating that as a violation of the user's intent is hyper-literal and misreads the constraint.

Verbose CLAUDE.md consumes session context — long sessions plus a heavy CLAUDE.md crowd out working memory
CLAUDE.md content is parsed only when /init is run; standing rules expire after the first hour
CLAUDE.md files over 10,000 words are silently truncated and most rules are dropped
feedbacks: Claude does not re-read CLAUDE.md every turn — it is loaded once at session start. The problem is total context budget, not a per-turn re-read step.

CLAUDE.md content counts against the context window. A 12,000-word file leaves less room for code, tool results, and reasoning, and as sessions extend the combined pressure causes earlier or middle content (including rules) to be deprioritized.
CLAUDE.md is reloaded at session start, not only at /init time, and there is no built-in expiration. The cause is context window economics.

prompt.question: A Code Generation team wants Claude to refactor a function while preserving public behavior. The prompt says 'Refactor for readability while keeping behavior the same.' Some refactors silently change function signatures. Which change MOST directly prevents signature changes?
answers: Lower temperature to 0 so refactors become more conservative
Explicitly forbid signature changes — 'Function name, parameter names, parameter order, and return type must remain identical'
Run the refactor through a linter after Claude finishes
Use prefilling to start with 'def ' and the original function name, since anchoring the opening tokens locks the signature to match the original
feedbacks: Conservativeness is not the same as signature preservation. The model can deterministically change signatures with low temperature.

'Keeping behavior the same' is interpretable; the model can treat signature changes as behavior-preserving if semantics are unchanged. Enumerating the four immutable signature attributes turns the rule into an explicit checklist the model can verify before responding.
A linter does not check signature equivalence with the original; only the prompt rule does. Linting is downstream of the issue.
Prefilling anchors the function name but not parameter order, names, or return type. Partial constraint, partial fix.
